title: Multiconfigurational Mixed Quantum-Classical Approach for Correlated Many-Body Dynamics
authors: Pritha Ghosh, Rajanya Sarkar, Arkajit Mandal
abstract: In this work, we introduce a multiconfigurational mixed quantum-classical many-body approach for simulating the finite-temperature correlated multi-exciton dynamics in the presence of phonon-induced static and dynamic disorder. In this mixed quantum-classical approach, the excitonic subsystem is described using a multiconfigurational wavefunction that extends beyond the mean-field limit, while the phonons are evolved quasi-classically. Using this approach, we simulate a multi-excitonic dissipative system and show how the interplay between phonon-induced dynamic disorder and exciton-exciton many-body interactions determines excitation-dependent excitonic transport and spatial correlations. Our results show that while the mean-field approach produces semi-quantitatively accurate diffusive dynamics, it does not capture the spatial correlations as expected. We find that a mean-field path approximation, where we generate pre-computed trajectories using our mean-field mixed quantum-classical approach and then perform multiconfigurational dynamics, can reproduce the spatial correlations to a good accuracy, positioning this approach as an efficient method for capturing spatial correlations in complex systems.
summary: The paper introduces a multiconfigurational mixed quantum-classical method to simulate complex exciton dynamics in disordered environments. It demonstrates that while standard mean-field approaches fail to capture essential spatial correlations, an efficient Mean-Field Path Approximation can successfully reproduce these many-body effects. This positions the approach as a powerful tool for studying correlated light-matter interactions in condensed matter systems.
main_problem: The work addresses simulating finite-temperature, correlated multi-exciton dynamics when coupled to phonons that induce both static and dynamic disorder.
main_result: A multiconfigurational mixed quantum-classical approach is proposed, showing that while mean-field methods fail to capture spatial correlations, a Mean-Field Path Approximation (MFPA) can accurately reproduce these crucial correlations.
method: The core method is a multiconfigurational mixed quantum-classical treatment where the excitonic subsystem uses a multiconfigurational wavefunction ansatz, and the lattice vibrations (phonons) are treated quasi-classically.
model_or_system: The system models interacting excitons on a lattice coupled to phonons, governed by an effective Hamiltonian involving Bose-Hubbard terms for excitons ($\hat{H}_e$) and phonon oscillators ($\hat{H}_p$).
key_observables: Excitonic transport (Mean Squared Displacement), spatial pair correlation function ($g^{(2)}(i, j)$), single-particle and two-particle reduced density matrices ($ho^{(1)}, ho^{(2)}$).
important_parameters: System parameters include hopping ($	au$), interaction strength ($U$), phonon coupling ($\gamma$), temperature ($T=150$ K), and disorder variance.
main_assumptions: The primary approximation is the Mean-Field Path Approximation (MFPA) used to efficiently capture spatial correlations, although this method is noted as insufficient for long-time transport dynamics.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the convergence of dynamics with increasing number of modes ($M$) and compare the evolution of the spatial pair correlation function $g^{(2)}$ between mean-field (low $M$) and multiconfigurational/MFPA results.
paper_structure: The paper details the derivation of coupled equations of motion for Single Particle Functions and expansion coefficients, implements numerical techniques like gauge fixing and re-orthonormalization, and then applies this framework to simulate dynamics under varying levels of quantum correlation inclusion ($M$).
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it tackles open quantum systems dynamics (excitons coupled to phonons) using advanced mixed quantum-classical techniques, providing systematic ways to recover strong correlations beyond simple mean-field limits.
